Nektar fell 22% Thursday to about $47 on long-term data for its alopecia treatment that looked good on the efficacy side. 
 
In the Phase 2b extension, 29% of patients on the low dose and 31% on the high dose had hair covering at least 80% of their scalps after a year on rezpegaldesleukin. Of those responders, 75% kept it four months after stopping treatment, and 63% at six months. 
 
The unusual part: hair kept growing off drug. The share with 90% scalp coverage rose to 19% six months after treatment ended, from 7% at the end of dosing. 
 
So why the selloff? Tolerability. William Blair's Andy Hsieh flagged 92% of patients had injection-site reactions vs 30% on placebo, plus more upper-respiratory infections and joint pain. His call: the adverse event "will pose an overhang" on the drug's profile. 
 
H.C. Wainwright read the same durability data as encouraging for rival Q32 Bio's bempikibart.

A jury said Eli Lilly owes Nektar Therapeutics 90 million dollars, plus interest. The verdict landed Thursday in the rezpegaldesleukin licensing fight (Sept 24, N.D. California). 
 
The number is two numbers. Nektar asked for 1 billion in damages; the jury gave it 90 million. Lilly's response: the verdict confirms it used commercially reasonable efforts and awarded only a small fraction of what Nektar sought. 
 
The backstory is the poison. Nektar alleged Lilly botched the trial analysis to make Rezpeg look weaker after buying competitor Dermira, giving it a pretext to walk. Lilly says Rezpeg simply missed the bar both sides had agreed to. 
 
Street split: BTIG reiterated Buy with a 178 target, calling the weakness a strong entry point. Wedbush cut its target to 50. 
 
Verdict subject to post-trial proceedings and appeal.
